source_title: Law Enforcement Use of Unmanned Aircraft Systems
regulated_activity: Use of a UAS by a law enforcement agency for surveillance, evidence-gathering, or other public-safety purposes
requirement_type: Prohibition with defined exceptions; agency procedural requirements
summary: AS 18.65.900 establishes a default prohibition: a law enforcement agency may not use a UAS except as provided in AS 18.65.900-18.65.909. AS 18.65.901 requires each agency to adopt written procedures covering FAA authorization, trained/certified pilots and supervising officials, sign-off by the commissioner/deputy commissioner of public safety or the agency's chief administrative officer, a public purpose, a logged auditable flight record, a public-notification method, and community involvement in developing the policy. AS 18.65.902 permits UAS use only (1) to gather evidence in a criminal investigation under a search warrant or a judicially recognized exception, or (2) for non-criminal uses that do not constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy and comply with the AS 18.65.901 procedures.

source_title: State of Alaska v. McKelvey (warrantless aerial surveillance with high-powered optics)
citation: State v. McKelvey, No. S-17910 (Alaska Mar. 8, 2024)
uas_topic: Aerial surveillance / privacy — constitutional framework relevant to UAS
regulated_party: Law enforcement (state constitutional holding; not a private-operator rule)
regulated_activity: Aerial photography/surveillance of private property using high-powered optics from an aircraft
requirement_type: Warrant requirement for aerial surveillance with optics that reveal details not visible to the naked eye
summary: The Alaska Supreme Court held that state troopers' warrantless aerial surveillance of a private backyard, using a zoom lens to photograph the property from an airplane, violated the search-and-seizure protections of the Alaska Constitution, because Alaskans have a reasonable expectation that authorities will not examine their property from the air using high-powered optics absent a warrant or recognized exception. The case facts involved a fixed-wing aircraft with a telephoto lens, not a UAS; however, a concurring opinion (Maassen, C.J., and Carney, J.) argued the court should have gone further and required a warrant for any aerial observation, and commentary on the decision (including from counsel who argued the case) explicitly frames it as relevant precedent for future drone-surveillance cases.

source_title: Unlawful Methods of Taking Game — Airborne/Remote/Wireless Spotting Devices
citation: 5 AAC 92.080(7)(G), (H), (I); carried into big-game methods at 5 AAC 92.085
effective_date: Effective July 1, 2025 (rule dates to 2014; subsequently amended)
regulated_activity: Using a UAS (or other airborne/remotely-controlled/wirelessly-communicating device with a camera or video device) to spot or locate game; using wireless communication to direct a hunter to a specific animal
requirement_type: Prohibition, with a same-day-plus cooling-off period
summary: 5 AAC 92.080(7)(G) makes it unlawful to take game with the aid of 'any device that has been airborne, controlled remotely, or communicates wirelessly, and is used to spot or locate game with the use of a camera or video device'; (7)(H) similarly bars any camera or sensory device that can send messages through wireless communication. (7)(I) adds that wireless communication may not be used to take a specific animal until 3:00 a.m. the day after the device was used (with narrow exceptions for specified bison and moose hunts using ground-based communication). This rule originated from a 2014 Board of Game action after Alaska Wildlife Troopers found hunters using drones to spot and assist in taking big game, and is carried into the big-game-specific methods list at 5 AAC 92.085.

summary: The Division's standard stipulations for Commercial Filming Permits include a dedicated 'Drone Use' provision (Stipulation 31) prohibiting drone operation in high-density public-use areas (campgrounds, picnic areas, trailheads, developed facilities); requiring FAR Part 107 compliance and FAA registration where required; capping altitude at 400 ft and requiring a 100 ft standoff from obstacles, people, or wildlife; requiring visual line of sight; barring flight near other aircraft, airports, or emergency-response efforts; prohibiting use to follow, chase, harass, or alter wildlife behavior; prohibiting use by anyone to spot game or assist another person's taking of game; and requiring the permittee to produce recorded images/video/data to law enforcement on request. status: Reviewed — no comprehensive UAS-specific preemption statute located
summary: Alaska has not enacted a comprehensive statewide UAS-preemption statute. Alaska's statewide UAS-specific statutes (AK-001) address only law-enforcement use, leaving room for municipalities to regulate private/recreational/commercial UAS use on locally controlled property. The Municipality of Anchorage, for example, restricts remote-control aircraft flight in its parks to designated areas (reported examples include Storck Park and Loretta French Park). Federal land managers (National Park Service units, national wildlife refuges) and the state's own Division of Parks and Outdoor Recreation (AK-004, AK-005) separately regulate takeoff/landing and operating conditions on the land they manage.
